title: Outline of a Tree
statement:
You get the root of a binary tree. Return the values on its outline, going counter-clockwise starting at the root:

  1. The root.
  2. The left edge, top to bottom. Start at root.left. From each node go to its left child if it has one, otherwise to its right child. Stop before the first leaf. If the root has no left child, the left edge is empty.
  3. All leaves of the tree, left to right.
  4. The right edge, bottom to top. It is the mirror rule: start at root.right, prefer the right child, stop before the first leaf, then reverse.

Every node appears at most once. The root counts as a leaf only when it is the only node.

Trees are written in level order with null for a missing child.

examples.why: Left edge: 2 (4 is a leaf, so it stops there). Leaves: 4, 7, 8, 6. Right edge from 3: 3 has no right child, so it would continue to 6, which is a leaf. 5 is on no edge but its leaves are.
The left edge turns right at 2 because 2 has no left child, then continues to 3. The right edge is empty because the root has no right child.
A lone root is listed once, not again as a leaf.

constraints: The tree is at most 500 levels deep
hints: Split the outline into three lists that do not overlap: the left edge without its leaf, all leaves, and the right edge without its leaf.
Each edge is a simple walk down: prefer one side, fall back to the other, stop when you reach a leaf. Leaves come from any left-to-right traversal.
Be careful with the root: it is never part of either edge walk or the leaf list unless it is the only node. Collect the right edge top-down, then reverse it.

explain.intuition:
Tracing the outline of a tree counter-clockwise is like running your finger down the left side, along the bottom, and back up the right side. Those are three separate pieces, and splitting the problem that way makes it easy.

The edges are plain loops: walk down preferring one side, falling back to the other when it is missing, and stop before a leaf so the leaf is not listed twice. The bottom is every leaf, found by a normal depth-first walk that visits left before right. The root is added once at the start, and the right edge is collected top-down and then reversed so it reads bottom-up.
steps: If the root is a leaf, return [root.val]. Otherwise start the result with root.val.
Walk from root.left: while the node is not a leaf, append it and move to left if present, else right.
Do a depth-first walk from the root and append every leaf, left subtree before right.
Walk from root.right the same way but preferring right, collecting non-leaf nodes into a separate list.
pitfalls: Taking only left children for the left edge. When a node on the edge has only a right child, the edge continues there, as in the second example.
Listing a leaf twice, once as the end of an edge and once among the leaves.
Treating the root as a leaf in the leaf pass when it has children, or as the start of the left edge when it has no left child.

complexity.space: O(h) for the walk, plus the output

solutions.title: Three passes: left edge, leaves, right edge
solutions.idea: Two simple loops for the edges and an explicit-stack DFS for the leaves.

solutions.title: One DFS with edge flags
solutions.idea: Pass down whether a node is on the left or right edge. Left-edge nodes are added before their children (top-down), right-edge nodes after them (bottom-up), leaves when reached.

followups: Return the outline clockwise instead. Which pieces swap and which get reversed?
Return the nodes visible from the left side of the tree (the first node on every level). How is that different from the left edge here?
